title: The free uniform spanning forest
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: A spanning tree of a finite connected graph, chosen with probability proportional to the product of weights on its edges. The first lesson proves the matrix-tree theorem with the formula of Cauchy and Binet, the expressions of the inclusion probabilities and covariances of edges through the inverse of the reduced Laplacian, the fact that different edges are never positively correlated, and the response identity: the absolute values of the derivatives of the inclusion probability of an edge with respect to the logarithms of all weights add up to 2p(1 - p), at most one half, for every graph and all weights. The second lesson constructs the free uniform spanning forest of an infinite connected graph in which every vertex lies on finitely many edges: the probability that a set of edges lies in the uniform spanning tree of a finite graph is a principal minor of the orthogonal projection onto the complement of the space of circulations; along an exhaustion by finite connected subgraphs these projections converge, and the laws of the uniform spanning trees converge to a probability measure that does not depend on the exhaustion, has no cycles and is carried along by isomorphisms of graphs. The third lesson studies the tilts of the forest by numbers on finitely many edges: a tilt is the conditional law given Gaussian observations of these edges; by the response identity the probability of an edge under a tilt changes by at most half the largest change of the numbers; the drift of an edge, the upper limit of these probabilities along the neighbourhoods of the edge, is a Borel function of all the numbers on the graph that satisfies the same bound and respects isomorphisms of graphs. The fourth lesson solves the integral equation Z = w + integral of b(s, Z(s)) ds for every family w of continuous paths on the edges, for a drift b that is Lipschitz for the supremum over the coordinates: existence and uniqueness by successive approximations, dependence only on the past, compatibility with relabellings, and measurability of the solution map; for the forest this defines a measurable map from families of paths to sets of edges. OpenAI's theorem (2026) is that this map sends independent Brownian motions to the free uniform spanning forest, which makes the forest a factor of independent labels; that step needs Brownian motion and is not yet in the course.
prerequisites: core course Linear Algebra (B40): determinants, expansion along a row, inverse matrices, symmetric matrices
core course Functional Analysis (D20): the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences, orthogonal projections onto closed subspaces

core course Measure and Integration (D10): Lebesgue measure and integral, monotone convergence, image measures, product measures and densities, measurable functions and their upper limits, the monotone class theorem and the uniqueness of a measure from its values on a generating family closed under intersections
the lessons prove every other fact they use

checks.reading: Lesson 1 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the lemma 'Weighted-tree response' in Section 2 of OpenAI's manuscript 'The free uniform spanning forest is a factor of IID' (25 Sep 2026); the introduction and Section 2 were read in full, Sections 3 to 6 not yet. Every step was derived; the lesson proves the Cauchy-Binet formula and the rank-one determinant formula, which the manuscript uses without proof. The identities (det L = Z, p_e = c_e a_e^T L^-1 a_e, Cov = -c_e c_f (a_e^T L^-1 a_f)^2, the row sum 2p(1 - p)) were checked in exact rational arithmetic on 40 random weighted connected graphs with up to 6 vertices. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 2 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the proposition 'Free exhaustion limit' in Section 2 of the manuscript. Every step was derived; the lesson adds the proofs of det(I + UV) = det(I + VU) and of the fact that a symmetric idempotent matrix is an orthogonal projection, the existence of exhaustions, and two examples. Before the lesson was written, the formula P(F in T) = det (K_H)_F was checked in exact rational arithmetic for 2,051 sets of edges on 25 random connected graphs, together with the symmetry, idempotence and trace of K_H. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 3 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the part 'Finite tilts and the canonical drift' of Section 2 and the first step of the lemma 'Posterior drift' in Section 3; Sections 3 and 4 of the manuscript were read in full on that day. Every step was derived; the lesson adds the statement and proof that a tilt is the conditional law given Gaussian observations at one time on finitely many coordinates, the proof that the neighbourhoods of an edge form an exhaustion, and four exercises. Checked numerically before staging (plan/checks_20261012/fu_check_tilts.py): the density identity; the response bound in 8,078 cases on 60 random graphs (largest ratio 0.85 of the bound); derivative equals covariance and the row sums of absolute covariances are at most 1/2 (largest 0.4988); the example with three equal coordinates; the formula for the triangle with three paths. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 4 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the lemma 'Deterministic inversion' in Section 4 of the manuscript; Section 5 was read in full on that day. Every step was derived; the lesson adds a proof of the measurability of integrals with a parameter, a proof that the evaluations generate the Borel sigma-algebra of the path space, a stability estimate, and a solved example in one coordinate. Checked numerically before staging (plan/checks_20261012/fu_check_inverse.py): the explicit solution of the example against a Runge-Kutta solution (deviation below 2e-11 on [0, 30]); the bound L^k t^(k+1)/(k+1)! for the successive approximations on a rough path, with L = 1/4 in one coordinate and L = 1/2 for the three edges of a triangle; the stability estimate. No discrepancy with the manuscript.

open_obligations: The main theorem of the manuscript (one Borel equivariant rule that produces the free uniform spanning forest from independent vertex labels on every infinite connected locally finite graph) is not proved in the course. The course contains the drift with its bound (lesson 3) and the solution map with the read-out of the slopes (lesson 4). Missing, with the foundations they need: (1) Brownian motion, countable families of independent Brownian motions, and the construction of such a family from independent uniform labels (Section 5, first lemma); (2) the posterior drift for observations in Brownian noise at all coordinates and the fact that the innovations are independent Brownian motions (Section 3; needs conditional expectations and the convergence of bounded martingales); (3) the measurability of the rule on the space of labelled graphs (Section 5); (4) for the last section, strongly Rayleigh measures. See plan/OPENAI_231_SCOPING_20261012.md.
